Writing to Hannah Arendt on 19 October 1949 about Nazi crimes and the question of guilt, Jaspers said that he took “things in all their banality, all their nothingness—bacteria can cause epidemics that destroy entire peoples and yet remain nothing more than bacteria.”
Hannah Arendt/Karl Jaspers, Briefwechsel 1926–1969, ed. Lotte Köhler and Hans Saner, Munich 1985, p. 99.
Walter Warnach — (1910–2000), writer and philosopher. The extensive correspondence between Warnach and Schmitt, covering 1948 to 1984, is forthcoming.

In a two-page letter dated 15 January 1949, Schmitt complains about attacks by Thieme and von der Heydte. He also suggests passing Warnach’s text on the Dominican priest R.-L. Bruckberger to Epting and contacting Father Laurentius Siemer in Cologne to arrange a meeting.
un livre de Amédée Ponceau — A. Ponceau, Timoléon. Réflexions sur la Tyrannie, preface by Louis Lavelle, introduction by Raymond Aron (Pensée et civilisation), Paris 1950.
A. Ponceau (1884–1948) was a French existentialist philosopher. Schmitt was also in contact with his widow, Michelle Ponceau, whose favorable reaction to ECS pleased him; see BW Mohler, p. 85.

Maiwald — Serge Maiwald (1916–1952), formerly Schmitt’s doctoral student and habilitation candidate. In 1946 he founded the Schriftenreihe der Universitas. Zeitschrift für Wissenschaft, Kunst und Literatur, which provided Schmitt with a publishing forum.

Schmitt had a particularly close friendship with Maiwald and dedicated to him the only obituary he ever wrote: Carl Schmitt, “Zum Gedächtnis an Serge Maiwald,” in Zeitschrift für Geopolitik 7 (1952), pp. 447–448. See also Günter Maschke’s notes to the republication in FoP, pp. 872–876; and below, p. 271.
Someone puts on the cap of invisibility … — This refers to Ernst Jünger’s novel Heliopolis.
Exposé by Father Bruckberger — Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger (1907–1998), French Dominican and member of the Resistance.
Laicus taceat in Ecclesia nisi clamat acclamationes praescriptas — “The layman is to remain silent in the Church except when uttering the prescribed acclamations.”

An allusion to 1 Corinthians 14:33–34: “As in all the congregations of the saints, women should remain silent in the churches; for they are not permitted to speak, but should be subordinate, as the law also says.”

Prussia, then, has been destroyed — The history of Prussia formally ended with Allied Control Council Law No. 46 of 25 February 1947. See above, p. 38: “Il n’y a plus de Prusse”—“There is no longer a Prussia.”
Dabitur donum fortitudinis — “The gift of courage will be given.” Refers to Thomas Aquinas; see Ulrich Horst, Die Gaben des Heiligen Geistes nach Thomas von Aquin, Berlin 2001, pp. 153 ff.
Father Franziskus Stratmann — (1883–1971), Dominican and representative of the Catholic peace movement.
Nous ne comparons pas les victimes, nous ne comparons que les juges — “We are not comparing the victims; we are comparing only the judges.”

Schmitt quotes from Lucien Laberthonnière, Sicut ministrator. Critique de la notion de souveraineté de la loi (Œuvres), Paris 1947, p. 84. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 27235.

On the importance of the Oratorian priest Laberthonnière (1860–1932) for Schmitt, see Schmitt’s essay “Das Problem der Legalität,” written around this time and originating in his interrogations by Kempner, in VA, pp. 440–451; first published in 1950 in Die neue Ordnung.

Summa contra Gentiles III 93 — For this quotation, Schmitt was using the following edition: Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra gentiles divi Thomae Aquinatis Angelici et v. ecclesiae doctoris … quatuor tributa libris de veritate catholicae fidei … volumen primum [-alterum] … Editio recens Parthenopeia ceteris cunctis accuratius a mendis expurgata de veritate catholicae fidei, vols. 1–2, Naples 1773 (RW 265 nos. 24547, 24548).

Cum infidelibus nec nomina debemus habere communia … — “We should not even have names in common with unbelievers, lest sharing the same names create an opportunity for error.” Thomas Aquinas, as above.
quoted in Privilege and Liberty — Aurel Kolnai, “Privilege and Liberty,” in Laval théologique et philosophique, vol. 5 (1949), p. 109.
Herr Ziemann’s idea — Ziemann was an editor at Heliopolisverlag in Tübingen.

Ernest Hello — (1828–1885), French writer and philosopher. The quotations can be found in E. Hello, Le siècle, les hommes et les idées, with a prefatory letter by Henri Lasserre, Paris 1896, pp. 365–367.
the Hamburg judgment against the German general Manstein — Erich von Manstein (1887–1973), field marshal, was convicted as a war criminal in 1949 by a British military court in Hamburg.
Causa victrix diis placuit — See above, note to p. 79.
Pulveris exigui sparget non longa vetustas / Congeriem, bustumque cadet, mortisque peribunt / Argumenta tuae.
“Before long, time will scatter the little heap of ashes; the tomb will collapse, and every sign of your death will disappear.”

my edition of the Pharsalia by Cortius — Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, Pharsalia sive de Bello Civili libri X. [Also included:] Eidemque adscriptum Carmen ad Pisonem [= Laus Pisonis], edited and emended in many places by Gottlieb Cortius, Leipzig 1726. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 27049.

The summary containing the expression scelus infandum—“unspeakable crime”—comes from the editor Cortius. The concept became important to Schmitt in connection with his 1945 legal opinion; see above, note to p. 66.
Smend wrote to me … — See BW Smend, pp. 123–124. Schmitt’s letter of 10 January 1950 appears there on p. 126.
To Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 243 ff.
the review Karl Korn … — K. Korn, “Der Sprung ins Wunderbare. Zu Ernst Jüngers neuem Buch ‘Heliopolis’,” in FAZ, 24 December 1949.
the kind of distrust that animates Herr de Mendelssohn — Refers to Peter de Mendelssohn, “Gegenstrahlungen. Ein Tagebuch zu Ernst Jüngers Tagebuch,” in Der Monat 2 (1949/50), no. 14, pp. 149–174.
“Then they remove them” — See above, note to p. 129.
Superos quid quaerimus ultra? — “Why look for the gods anywhere else?” Pharsalia, IX, 579.
Salus ex Judaeis? Perditio ex Judaeis? — “Salvation from the Jews? Destruction from the Jews?” Compare Vulgate, John 4:22. See also above, note to p. 153.
Spinoza was the first to slip himself in — See Leviathan, pp. 86 ff.

opus operatum — A concept from the Catholic doctrine of the sacraments. For Catholics, a sacrament administered by an ordained priest works ex opere operato—by virtue of the rite having been performed—and therefore does not depend on the personal worthiness or unworthiness of the priest who administers it.
favor victoris — “the favor of the victor.”
Porzia method — Refers to the Roman Lex Porcia; see above, note to p. 108.
Anyone who comments on himself falls below his own level — Quotation from Ernst Jünger’s Blätter und Steine (1934). See also BW EJ, p. 280.
Jünger’s two letters — Not dated the 10th and 16th, but the 13th and 16th of January; see BW EJ, pp. 246 ff. See also below, note to p. 373.

Ch. Journet — Charles Journet (1891–1975), Swiss Catholic theologian and cardinal. Schmitt has the following title in mind: Charles Journet, L’Église du Verbe incarné. Essai de théologie spéculative. 1. La hiérarchie apostolique, [Paris] 1941.
Cum armis Jherusalem peregrinati sunt — “They went armed on pilgrimage to Jerusalem.” Quotation from the Gesta Francorum, an account of the First Crusade. See also Nomos, p. 27, note 2.

Bellorum quippe ac proeliorum certamina … — “The struggles of wars and battles are not merely the beginning of all deceptions; through deception they are also, in fact, discoveries of the arts of the devil.”
From Monumenta Germaniae historica inde ab anno Christi quingentesimo usque ad annum millesimum et quingentesimum: Epistolarum, vol. 6/1, Epistolae Karolini aevi, Berlin 1939, p. 585.

Il n’y a pas moyen d’expliquer comment … — Schmitt quotes from Joseph de Maistre, Les soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg, ou entretiens sur le gouvernement temporel de la providence. Suivis d’un traité sur les sacrifices, vols. 1–2, Paris 1821. The passage is in vol. 2, p. 2. Correctly:
“…il n’y a pas moyen d’expliquer comment la guerre est possible humainement.”
“…there is no way to explain how war is humanly possible.”
châtiment divin; divine au sens où l’enfer est divin — Quotation from Charles Journet, L’Église du Verbe incarné, vol. 1: La hiérarchie apostolique, 3rd ed., [Paris] 1962, p. 621. Correctly:
“la guerre apparaît comme un châtiment divin, elle est divine au sens où l’enfer est divin.”
“War appears as a divine punishment; it is divine in the sense that hell is divine.”

Primo, quod ipsa peccata, quibus Deus indignatus implevit tantis calamitatibus mundum, humiliter cogitantes, quamvis longe absint a facinorosis, flagitiosis atque impiis, tamen non usque adeo se a delictis deputant alienos, ut nec temporalia pro eis mala perpeti se judicent dignos.

“First, when they humbly reflect on the sins because of which God, in his anger, has filled the world with so many calamities, they do not imagine themselves so free of fault that they believe they deserve no temporal suffering for their own sins—even though they are far removed from the criminal, vicious, and godless.”
Augustine, The City of God (De civitate Dei), trans. Wilhelm Thimme, introduction and commentary by Carl Andresen, vol. 1, Munich 1977, p. 15.
Après avoir lu cette description de la guerre juste … — Ch. Journet, op. cit., p. 623.
Carl Erdmann claims — In Die Entstehung des Kreuzzugsgedankens; see p. 223.
Batiffol — Pierre Batiffol, Le catholicisme de Saint Augustin, Paris 1920.
Gustave Schnürer — Gustav Schnürer, L’Église et la civilisation au Moyen-âge, vol. I, trans. G. Castella and Mme M.-Th. Burgard, preface by Édouard Jordan, Paris 1933.
Godenholm — Ernst Jünger, Besuch auf Godenholm, Frankfurt am Main 1952.
Not every kind of food is advisable for those who dream — In a letter to Nicolaus Sombart dated 2 May 1950, Schmitt gives the correct wording of this line from Georg Britting’s poem “Der Fasan”:
“About Sartre, only this line: Not every feast is advisable for those who dream.”
Son of this consecration … — Adapted from a line by Theodor Däubler in the poem “Am Meere,” from the collection Der sternhelle Weg. The original reads:
“Son of this consecration, you ought to tremble! Listen and suffer.”

Rousseau speaks of the stake … — “The first man who fenced off a piece of land, thought of saying ‘This is mine,’ and found people simple enough to believe him was the true founder of civil society. How many crimes, wars, murders, miseries, and horrors might the human race have been spared by someone who pulled up the stakes or filled in the ditch and cried out to his fellow men: ‘Beware of listening to this impostor; you are lost if you forget that the fruits of the earth belong to everyone, and the earth itself to no one.’”

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Diskurs über die Ungleichheit. Discours sur l’inégalité, critical edition of the complete text with all fragments and supplementary materials, newly edited, translated, and annotated by Heinrich Meier, Paderborn 1984, p. 173.
In 1926 I wrote and published … — C. Schmitt, Die Kernfrage des Völkerbundes, Berlin 1926; reprinted in FoP, pp. 98–99, note 37.
the work by the young Hegel — See above, note to p. 50.
Ah, no bodily wing will join the wings of the spirit — Correctly:
“Ah! To the wings of the spirit no bodily wing will so easily be joined.”

In the so-called Hochland it is getting more oppressive all the time — In the journal Hochland in 1950, Else Lasker-Schüler’s poem “Ich weiß” appears on p. 352, while Konrad Weiß’s meditation on Maria Caspar-Filser’s painting “Rosen in blauer Vase” appears after p. 568.

Weinreich — Paul Weinreich (1906–1974), editor at the Hanseatische Verlagsanstalt and, from 1946 onward, publisher of Deutsches Zeit-Archiv. Presseberichte und Zeitungsausschnittsdienst. Schmitt received Edition B, devoted to cultural news.
